newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens comm sales rise 18 pct.
newsitem.headline: Siemens comm sales rise 18 pct.

text.p: German giant Siemens AG, citing expanding product palettes, said on Thursday its communications businesses saw sales rise 18 percent to 9.5 billion marks ($5.6 billion) in the first five months of business year 1996/97.

New orders in its public and private networks units and its defense electronics group rose 20 percent to 12.1 billion in the period, said management board member Volker Jung at the CeBIT trade fair here.
Aggressive product development -- along with international expansion -- was critical to ensure the rapid rate of growth continues, Jung said.

"There is hardly a company anywhere like Siemens with a full portfolio of telecommunications products," he said at a news conference. "This makes us a system integrator for communications, capable of providing worldwide solutions from a single source."
But Jung also said it was still taking too long for Siemens to develop new products, especialy software that adds new capabilities to its phones, switches and networking devices.
Profits would increase as sales climb over the next several years, he said.

Public networks (ON), which sells switches, cables and other gear to phone companies, saw sales in the five-month period since September 30 rise 26 percent to five billion marks while orders increased 26 percent to 7.4 billion marks.
Private networks (PN), which makes cordless, cellular and standard telephone sets, saw sales in the period climb 15 percent to four billion marks and orders 14 percent to 4.2 billion marks.
Jung said PN is the world's top supplier of telephone sets, while ON equipment routed one tenth of all calls worldwide.
He gave no figures for the defence electronics business, for which Siemens was seeking a buyer or joint venture partner.
At CeBIT, Siemens was demonstrating some of the new products it would count on to keep sales on the incline, Jung said. One was the SL10 mini cellular digital phone that was due next year.
Siemens was also demonstrating an "asymmetric digital subscriber line" (ASDL), which would send data 300 times faster over copper phone cables than today's standard modems.
To make it easier for people to place phone calls over the Internet, Siemens was developing a switch that could route calls from the Internet to conventional phone networks, Jung said.
This Internetworking Unit would mean Internet phone calls could go to anyone, not just others who have computers on the Internet, Jung said.

The InterXpress messaging system, due in the fall, could create "universal mailboxes" that would store voice messages, faxes and electronic mail in one machine. People would be able to retrieve the messages with computers, fax machines or standard telephones, he said.
"All highly industrialised countries are undergoing fundamental changes," he said. "The most visible expression of this change is certainly the Internet."

Many of these new products would help Siemens expand outside of Germany. Soon after the turn of the century, Europe would only account for one fifth of the world's electronics markets, compared to one third today.
"The most important growth regions today are America, Eastern Europe and Asia-Pacific," he said.
Siemens planned to build production centers in these regions and to pursue a "rigorous strategy of acqusitions and cooperations" to break into new markets, he said.
